newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden risks loss of EU influence over EMU.
newsitem.headline: Sweden risks loss of EU influence over EMU.

text.p: Sweden risks losing influence in the European Union if, as widely expected, it decides not to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at its planned launch in 1999, diplomats and analysts say.
They believe such a move may reduce Stockholm's clout even on EU issues not directly linked to the single currency, such as eastern enlargement -- a key Swedish priority.
"It is clear that our voice will carry less weight," said Carl Hamilton, chief economist at Handelsbanken in Stockholm.
"It will become more difficult for us to assert our own interests, and that goes for all areas."
An EU diplomat took a similar line. "You are not as relevant as a discussion partner if you are not in the inner circle."

Sweden's ruling Social Democrats, struggling with a considerable number of eurosceptics both in the party and among the Swedish public, are expected to come out soon against joining monetary union from the start, even if the country fulfils the economic criteria.
The party leadership may decide its position on EMU at a scheduled meeting on Friday.
An extraordinary party congress will then vote on the issue in September. Parliament's decision follows later in the autumn.

The finance ministry on Wednesday dismissed as speculation a radio report saying Finance Minister Erik Asbrink and Prime Minister Goran Persson did not want to join EMU during the 1998-2002 term without new elections being held.
A decision to delay membership may cause irritation in other EU capitals as Sweden does not have the same formal right as Denmark and Britain under the Maastricht treaty to opt out from EMU.
"It will be seen as though Sweden is not keeping its part of the deal," one EU diplomat said.
However, EU officials have conceded that a country can not be forced to join against its will, joking that the European Commission would not send tanks into the streets of Stockholm.
Asbrink said this week he did not believe the country's EMU decision would be met with protests from its EU partners.
He said he had explained Sweden's specific problems to his EU colleagues at international meetings in recent months.
"I'm convinced that they will receive it (the decision) with understanding," he told the Swedish news agency TT in Paris.
After voting for EU membership in 1994, many Swedes have turned against Brussels, which they blame for economic austerity measures.
Analysts said the decision's wording would be a crucial factor in determining its impact on Sweden's EU standing.

Persson faces the difficult task of striking a politically delicate balance between the needs of financial markets and EMU supporters and the demands of those sceptical of or against the single currency.
Hamilton said the negative effect would be limited if the decision was seen as only a temporary delay in joining EMU.
But if Sweden were to say that it was uncertain about ever entering, the consequences would become more problematic, he said.
"They are likely to try to find a soft way of saying that (Sweden) will not join immediately," said political science professor Olof Ruin at Stockholm University.
However, the Swedish situation may change fast if Britain takes steps to join monetary union in the next few years.
"If Britain moves towards EMU membership, it will be of decisive significance for Sweden," said Hamilton.
